column1: {{c1::Object-level permissions}} determine which operations a principal can perform on a specific database object.
column2:
RLS instead restricts which rows are accessible within protected objects.
Review source

column1: The unit's main permission scopes narrow from server to database to {{c1::schema}} to object.
column2:
Permissions at broader scopes can imply rights at narrower scopes.
Review source

column1: Grant schema-wide reading with GRANT SELECT ON {{c1::SCHEMA}}::Sales TO SalesAnalyst;
column2:
The grant covers current and future tables and views, subject to applicable denials.
Review source

column1: Use GRANT {{c1::EXECUTE}} ON SCHEMA::Reports TO ReportingUsers; to allow procedure execution in Reports.
column2:
The schema-level permission also covers future procedures in the schema.
Review source

column1: Allow reading dbo.Customers with {{c1::GRANT SELECT}} ON dbo.Customers TO CustomerServiceRole;
column2:
This grants a specific data operation on the named table.
Review source

column1: For a non-owner outside sysadmin, conflicting table-level grants and denials from different roles resolve to {{c1::DENY}}.
column2:
This does not describe the separate column-level GRANT exception.
Review source

column1: Remove an explicit permission assignment without creating a denial by using {{c1::REVOKE}}.
column2:
It can remove a GRANT or DENY, while permissions from other sources can remain.
Review source

column1: In SQL Server, a table-level SELECT DENY does not override a {{c1::column-level SELECT GRANT}}.
column2:
This is a documented backward-compatibility exception to normal denial precedence.
Review source

column1: Create a user-defined database role with {{c1::CREATE ROLE}} DataReaders;
column2:
Assign job-specific permissions to the role.
Review source

column1: Add a database user to a role with ALTER ROLE DataReaders {{c1::ADD MEMBER}} JohnSmith;
column2:
Membership supplies the role's permissions to the user.
Review source

column1: A user-defined role nested inside another role inherits the {{c1::containing role's permissions}}.
column2:
For ALTER ROLE Readers ADD MEMBER Writers, Writers' members receive Readers' permissions.
Review source

column1: GRANT {{c1::CONTROL}} ON SCHEMA::HR TO HRAdministrators; gives broad control within the HR schema.
column2:
It is not a grant of CONTROL over the whole database.
Review source

column1: With Entra authentication configured in Azure SQL Database, create the identity's user with CREATE USER [MyWebApp] {{c1::FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER}};
column2:
The identity must also receive the database permissions required by the application.
Review source

column1: Obtaining an Entra access token does not automatically grant {{c1::database permissions}}.
column2:
Authentication identifies the caller, while authorization determines allowed operations.
Review source

column1: Microsoft Entra authentication support begins with SQL Server {{c1::2022 (16.x)}}.
column2:
Configure the required identity integration before using it.
Review source

column1: SQL database in Microsoft Fabric supports {{c1::Microsoft Entra authentication only}}.
column2:
It does not support SQL authentication or SQL logins.
Review source

column1: An Azure managed identity removes the need for the application to manage a {{c1::password or client secret}} for authentication.
column2:
Azure manages the identity's credentials, but its host and tokens still require protection.
Review source

column1: A {{c1::system-assigned}} managed identity shares the lifecycle of its Azure host resource.
column2:
Deleting that resource deletes the identity.
Review source

column1: A {{c1::user-assigned}} managed identity is an independent resource that multiple supported Azure hosts can share.
column2:
Its lifecycle is separate from the hosts that use it.
Review source

column1: In Microsoft.Data.SqlClient 2.1+, select managed identity with Authentication={{c1::Active Directory Managed Identity}}.
column2:
The application host must expose the identity, and the target database must authorize it.
Review source

column1: For App Service-to-Azure SQL authentication, enable the managed identity on the {{c1::application host}}.
column2:
Enabling an identity on the database server does not supply the application's calling identity.
Review source

column1: In SqlClient, {{c1::Encrypt}}=True requests encryption of client-server traffic.
column2:
Keep certificate validation enabled as a separate protection.
Review source

column1: With Encrypt=True, keep normal SqlClient certificate validation enabled using {{c1::TrustServerCertificate}}=False.
column2:
Bypassing validation leaves the server's identity unverified.
Review source

column1: Store password-bearing connection strings in protected configuration such as {{c1::Azure Key Vault}}, not source code.
column2:
Managed identities avoid placing an application password or client secret in the connection string.
Review source

column1: If an application must use a service-principal client secret, store it securely and {{c1::rotate it regularly}}.
column2:
Remove superseded secrets when they are no longer needed.
Review source

column1: When managed identity is unavailable, an application can use a {{c1::client certificate}} instead of a shared client secret.
column2:
The certificate's private key still needs protection and lifecycle management.
Review source

column1: Inspect explicit database permission assignments through {{c1::sys.database_permissions}}.
column2:
The view is not a complete list of every user's effective permissions.
Review source

column1: Check the caller's effective permissions with SELECT * FROM {{c1::fn_my_permissions}}('Sales.Orders', 'OBJECT');
column2:
Effective permissions include rights obtained through roles and broader permission scopes.
Review source

column1: In sys.database_permissions, class = {{c1::1}} identifies OBJECT_OR_COLUMN permissions for an object-ID join.
column2:
Other classes use major_id for different kinds of securables.
Review source

column1: The built-in permissions of {{c1::fixed database roles}} do not appear in sys.database_permissions.
column2:
Do not treat a catalog query of explicit assignments as the complete effective permission set.
Review source

column1: The fixed role {{c1::db_datareader}} permits reading all user tables and views in the database.
column2:
A custom schema-scoped role can provide narrower access.
Review source

column1: The fixed role {{c1::db_datawriter}} permits INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE on all user tables.
column2:
It does not itself grant SELECT.
Review source
